set1.q: A 50-year-old woman with symptomatic varicose veins has worn stockings and exercised faithfully for several months with persistent aching. Duplex ultrasound confirms great saphenous vein reflux. Which is the most appropriate next treatment?
opts: Surgical valvuloplasty

Valvuloplasty is only occasionally successful and carries a high incidence of postoperative deep vein thrombosis. Superficial saphenous reflux after failed stockings is treated with venous ablation, by laser or radiofrequency catheter, rather than valve repair.
Venous ablation therapy

Correct. A trial of conservative therapy with stockings is generally done for weeks to months before venous ablation therapy is offered. She has completed that trial with persistent aching and duplex confirms great saphenous reflux, so ablation, whose goal is better symptoms and appearance, comes next.
Lifelong observation only

Observation alone leaves her persistent aching untreated after several months of faithful stockings and exercise. Once a trial of conservative therapy has failed, venous ablation therapy is offered to improve symptoms and appearance.
Oral flavonoid therapy

Flavonoids are used to increase venous tone, but no oral medication has yet been proven useful for venous disease. After a failed trial of stockings with confirmed saphenous reflux, the next step is venous ablation therapy.

set1.q: A 52-year-old man starts outpatient treatment for deep vein thrombosis with low molecular weight heparin injections overlapped with warfarin. The injections continue for at least five days and until his international normalized ratio is above which value?
opts: Above 1

Above 1 is too low a target; the overlap of injections with warfarin continues for at least 5 days and until the international normalized ratio is above 2. Stopping at a value just above 1 ends the heparin before warfarin has reached the required level.
Above 2

Correct. For outpatient treatment, low molecular weight heparin (enoxaparin) or fondaparinux is given for at least 5 days, overlapping with warfarin, until the international normalized ratio (INR) is above 2. Inpatient unfractionated heparin uses the same cutoff, overlapping warfarin until the INR has been above 2 for at least 24 hours.
Above 3

Above 3 overshoots the threshold. The heparin and warfarin overlap ends after at least 5 days once the international normalized ratio is above 2, so waiting for 3 would extend the injections beyond what is required.
Above 4

Above 4 is well past the threshold. The overlap continues for at least 5 days and until the international normalized ratio is above 2, the same cutoff used when unfractionated heparin is overlapped with warfarin in hospital.

set1.q: A 45-year-old woman has a catheter-related deep vein thrombosis of the right arm and asks how likely a pulmonary embolism is compared with a leg clot. Which statement is accurate?
opts: Up to 6%, versus 15 to 30% for leg clots

Correct. Pulmonary embolism occurs in up to 6% of upper-extremity deep vein thromboses (DVTs), versus 15% to 30% of lower-extremity ones, so her catheter-related arm clot carries the lower risk. Arm clots are only 5% to 10% of all DVTs and are most often caused by pacemakers, defibrillators or central venous catheters.
15 to 30%, versus up to 6% for leg clots

This reverses the two figures. Pulmonary embolism complicates 15% to 30% of lower-extremity deep vein thromboses and only up to 6% of upper-extremity ones, so her arm clot carries the lower risk, not the higher.
About 3% for arm and leg clots alike

About 3% for both sites ignores that the risk differs by location. Pulmonary embolism occurs in up to 6% of upper-extremity clots like her catheter-related one, but in 15% to 30% of lower-extremity clots; the tell is that leg clots carry several times the risk.
Under 1% for arm clots, 6% for leg clots

Both numbers are too low, and the leg figure is off most: pulmonary embolism occurs in 15% to 30% of lower-extremity clots, not 6%. Up to 6% is the figure for upper-extremity clots like hers, so this choice moves the arm number onto the leg.

set1.q: A 68-year-old woman with active pancreatic cancer, which supplies the hypercoagulable component of the Virchow triad, has an acute proximal deep vein thrombosis of the left leg. She also has active gastrointestinal bleeding. Which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Systemic thrombolysis

Thrombolysis with tissue plasminogen activator is helpful for a large proximal deep vein thrombosis or a stable pulmonary embolism, but it dissolves clot and she is actively bleeding. An acute proximal clot with active hemorrhage is the setting for an inferior vena cava filter.
Outpatient rivaroxaban

Rivaroxaban is an anticoagulant, and the most serious adverse effect of anticoagulation is hemorrhage. With active gastrointestinal bleeding and an acute proximal clot, an inferior vena cava filter is used instead of anticoagulation.
Inferior vena cava filter

Correct. An inferior vena cava filter is used only when a patient has an acute proximal lower extremity deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and active bleeding, or when anticoagulation is otherwise contraindicated. She has both an acute proximal clot and active gastrointestinal bleeding.
Unfractionated heparin infusion

Unfractionated heparin is an anticoagulant, and hemorrhage is the most serious adverse effect of anticoagulation, so it would add to her active bleeding. An acute proximal clot with active bleeding is the indication for an inferior vena cava filter.

set1.q: A 50-year-old man developed a single large arteriovenous fistula of the forearm after a penetrating injury. It causes swelling and a bruit over the arm. Which is the management for this acquired fistula?
opts: Surgical removal or size reduction

Correct. His fistula is acquired, from a penetrating injury, and is a single large connection. Acquired arteriovenous (AV) fistulas are managed surgically, by removing the fistula or decreasing its size; elastic support hose and embolization are the approaches described for congenital fistulas.
Compression stockings alone

Elastic support hose is the conservative treatment for congenital fistulas, which are hard to treat because their communications can be numerous. His is a single large fistula acquired from a penetrating injury, so it is managed surgically by removal or size reduction.
Warm compresses and elevation

Warm compresses and elevation do not treat an artery-to-vein connection. The tell is the cause: a fistula acquired from injury is corrected surgically, by removing it or decreasing its size, while a congenital one with numerous communications is managed conservatively with elastic support hose.
Lifelong anticoagulation alone

Anticoagulation does not close or shrink an abnormal artery-to-vein connection, and nothing here describes a clot. A fistula acquired from a penetrating injury, like his, is managed surgically by removing the fistula or decreasing its size.

set1.q: A 55-year-old man with symptomatic varicose veins has a duplex ultrasound showing significant saphenous vein reflux. Which referral is most appropriate?
opts: Vascular specialist

Correct. Significant saphenous reflux is one of the reasons to refer to a vascular specialist, along with arterial insufficiency, nonhealing or recurrent ulcers, persistent stasis dermatitis and diagnostic uncertainty. Varicose veins usually involve the great saphenous vein, so his reflux sits in the vein most often affected.
Cardiologist

A cardiologist is not the referral for superficial venous reflux; his problem is in the leg veins, usually the great saphenous vein in varicose veins. Significant saphenous reflux is one of the triggers for referral to a vascular specialist.
Hematologist

A hematologist does not manage saphenous reflux, which arises from venous reflux and venous hypertension in the leg veins rather than from a blood disorder. Referral to a vascular specialist is indicated for significant saphenous reflux.
Orthopedic surgeon

An orthopedic surgeon does not treat venous reflux. Significant saphenous reflux on duplex ultrasound is a reason for referral to a vascular specialist, who can consider surgery aimed at restoring proper flow and lowering venous hypertension.

set1.q: A 69-year-old man receiving an unfractionated heparin infusion for deep vein thrombosis develops life-threatening bleeding. Which agent reverses the heparin?
opts: Protamine sulfate

Correct. He is on an unfractionated heparin (UFH) infusion and has life-threatening bleeding, the most serious adverse effect of anticoagulation. Protamine sulfate is the reversal agent for UFH and for low molecular weight heparin.
Idarucizumab
Idarucizumab is the reversal agent for dabigatran and does not reverse heparin. For life-threatening bleeding on an unfractionated heparin infusion, the reversal agent is protamine sulfate.
Andexanet alfa

Andexanet alfa reverses apixaban and rivaroxaban, with off-label use for edoxaban; it is not the antidote for heparin. His bleeding on an unfractionated heparin infusion is reversed with protamine sulfate.
Vitamin K by mouth

Oral vitamin K is one of the reversal options for warfarin, alongside prothrombin complex concentrate and fresh frozen plasma. He is bleeding on an unfractionated heparin infusion, which is reversed with protamine sulfate.

set1.q: A 74-year-old man with diabetes has a painful ulcer over the lateral ankle. His foot is cool and the pedal pulses are weak. Which test should be obtained next?
opts: Punch biopsy of the ulcer

A punch biopsy helps rule out other causes when the cause of an ulcer is uncertain. Here the painful lateral ulcer with weak pulses already points to arterial insufficiency, so the ankle-brachial index comes first.
Ankle-brachial index

Correct. A painful ulcer usually on the lateral aspect of the ankle with weak pulses fits arterial insufficiency, and he is older with a lower extremity wound. Arterial pulse examination combined with the ankle-brachial index (ABI) should be performed on any such patient.
Venous duplex ultrasound

Venous duplex ultrasound assesses venous patency and valve reflux, the questions for a suspected venous ulcer. His painful lateral ulcer with a cool foot and weak pulses is an arterial picture, assessed with the ankle-brachial index.
Catheter-based venography

Catheter-based venography is the invasive gold standard for the veins, rarely needed for diagnosis and done before an intervention. It does not assess the arterial supply suggested by his weak pulses and painful lateral ulcer.

set1.q: A 44-year-old man develops a first calf deep vein thrombosis one week after minor knee arthroscopy under a local nerve block, followed by a long car trip. Which duration of anticoagulation is appropriate?
opts: A fixed three months

Three months is the course for a clot provoked by a major transient factor, such as surgery under general anesthesia over 30 minutes, bed rest of 3 days or more, or major trauma or fracture. His minor arthroscopy under a nerve block and a long car trip are minor factors, which call for 3 to 6 months.
Indefinitely

Indefinite anticoagulation is for an unprovoked first venous thromboembolism, one with no identifiable risk factor. His clot followed minor surgery and a long car trip, identifiable minor transient factors that call for 3 to 6 months.
Six weeks

Six weeks falls below the minimum: every patient with an acute first venous thromboembolism (deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism) is anticoagulated for at least 3 months. His minor-factor clot calls for 3 to 6 months.
Three to six months

Correct. Minor surgery and prolonged travel are both minor transient risk factors, and a first venous thromboembolism (VTE) provoked by a minor transient factor is treated for 3 to 6 months. His arthroscopy used a local nerve block, not general anesthesia over 30 minutes, so it is not a major factor.

set1.q: A 42-year-old woman has symptomatic varicose veins that did not improve with stockings. She prefers a nonsurgical procedure in which a solution is injected to scar and close the veins. Which procedure fits?
opts: Vein stripping
Vein stripping is a surgical reflux treatment that removes the vein; nothing is injected. The procedure that injects a sclerosing agent to fibrose and obliterate the veins is sclerotherapy.
Radiofrequency ablation
Radiofrequency treatment is delivered by catheter as a surgical reflux treatment, not by injecting a solution. The injection of a sclerosing agent to fibrose and obliterate veins is sclerotherapy.
Venous bypass

Venous bypass is not an injection and is not among the varicose vein interventions, which are sclerotherapy, stripping and catheter ablation. Injecting a sclerosing agent to close the veins is sclerotherapy.
Sclerotherapy

Correct. Sclerotherapy injects a sclerosing agent to fibrose and obliterate the veins, matching her wish for an injection that scars and closes them. It is offered after a trial of conservative therapy with stockings, which she has had.

set1.q: A 24-year-old soccer player comes to urgent care with left calf pain that began two days ago when he felt a sudden pull while sprinting, and he has bruising around the ankle. He has no leg swelling, tenderness along the deep veins, cancer, cast or history of clots. By the Wells criteria, a calf muscle tear is at least as likely as deep vein thrombosis. Which is the most appropriate first test?
opts: D-dimer blood test

Correct. He has no positive Wells items, and a calf muscle tear at least as likely as deep vein thrombosis (DVT) subtracts 2, so his score is minus 2, a low likelihood (zero or less). Low-risk patients start with a D-dimer, which is sensitive: a negative result stops the work-up, and only a positive one leads to ultrasound.
Venous duplex ultrasound

Venous duplex ultrasound comes first only for a high-risk patient, or after a positive D-dimer in a low-risk one. His likelier alternative diagnosis puts his Wells score at zero or below, so a D-dimer comes first and a negative result ends the evaluation.
Contrast ascending venography

Contrast ascending venography is the definitive gold standard, but it has been replaced by venous duplex ultrasound and is not a first test. For a low-likelihood score like his, the pathway begins with a D-dimer and moves to imaging only if it is positive.
Computed tomography of the leg

Computed tomography of the leg is not part of the initial pathway for suspected deep vein thrombosis, which runs from the Wells score to a D-dimer or ultrasound. For his low-likelihood score the first step is a D-dimer, with ultrasound reserved for a positive result.

set1.q: A 27-year-old woman has a first deep vein thrombosis of the left leg. Genetic testing shows factor V Leiden, an inherited clotting abnormality. Which component of the Virchow triad does this finding represent?
opts: Venous insufficiency

Venous insufficiency is listed under venous stasis, the altered blood flow component, along with immobilization and heart failure. Factor V Leiden is a genetic change in clotting, an inherited hypercoagulable state.
Hypercoagulable state

Correct. Factor V Leiden is an inherited hypercoagulable state, listed with prothrombin gene mutation and protein C, protein S or antithrombin deficiency. In the Virchow triad it represents a clotting tendency of the blood, separate from stasis or vessel injury.
Venous stasis

Venous stasis is altered blood flow from immobilization, venous insufficiency or heart failure. Her finding is a genetic clotting abnormality, which the triad places under the hypercoagulable state, inherited or acquired.
Endothelial trauma

Endothelial injury comes from trauma, surgery, intravenous drug use or burns. Factor V Leiden is a gene finding that changes the blood's clotting tendency, which makes it an inherited hypercoagulable state.

set1.q: A 66-year-old man has long-standing pitting edema of the lower leg with brown pigmentation and a healed medial ankle ulcer. Duplex ultrasound shows thickened, scarred valve leaflets and chronic obstruction of the femoral vein. He does not recall any leg clot. Which is the most likely cause of his condition?
opts: Congenital arteriovenous fistula

A congenital or acquired arteriovenous fistula is one of the less common causes of chronic venous insufficiency. Thickened, scarred leaflets with chronic femoral vein obstruction are post-thrombotic changes, so this is secondary disease from a prior deep vein thrombosis, even without a remembered clot.
Pelvic vein neoplastic obstruction

Neoplastic obstruction of the pelvic veins is listed only among the other, less common causes. His duplex shows scarred valve leaflets and chronic obstruction of the femoral vein, the post-thrombotic findings that point to a prior deep vein thrombosis.
Prior deep vein thrombosis

Correct. Thickened, scarred valve leaflets with chronic obstruction of the femoral vein are the post-thrombotic picture, and prior deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is one of the most common causes of chronic venous insufficiency. Not recalling a clot does not exclude it: about 25% of these patients have no known history of DVT.
Progressive superficial reflux

Progressive superficial venous reflux is another common cause, but in it the valves fail because they sit in a dilated vein. His leaflets are thickened and scarred with chronic proximal obstruction, which is the post-thrombotic pattern of a prior deep vein thrombosis.

set1.q: A 34-year-old woman has visible, dilated, tortuous veins of the thigh and calf that are tender to palpation, with aching heaviness after prolonged standing. Which is the most common predisposing factor for her condition?
opts: Recent pregnancy
Women are at higher risk after pregnancy, so a recent pregnancy is a recognized contributor. The question asks for the most common predisposing factor, and that is family history, not pregnancy.
Regular heavy lifting

Heavy lifting causes periods of high venous pressure and is a real risk factor for varicose veins, but it is not the most common one. Family history is named the most common predisposing factor, so it outranks lifting even in a patient who lifts.
Family history of varicose veins

Correct. Her dilated, tortuous, tender thigh and calf veins with aching heaviness after standing describe varicose veins. Among the risk factors, family history is named the most common predisposing factor for unwanted leg veins, ahead of prolonged standing, heavy lifting and pregnancy.
Prolonged standing at work

Prolonged standing produces periods of high venous pressure and also brings on her aching, but it is a contributing risk factor rather than the most common one. Family history is named the most common predisposing factor for unwanted leg veins.

set1.q: A 59-year-old woman had a left leg deep vein thrombosis 11 months ago. She now has chronic left leg heaviness, edema and brownish ankle skin that worsen with standing and improve with elevation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Recurrent deep vein thrombosis

A new clot would bring swelling, pain, warmth or erythema, often with a calf cramp that worsens over a few days. Her complaints are chronic, ease with elevation and began 11 months after the first clot, the course of post-thrombotic syndrome rather than recurrence.
Lymphedema

Lymphedema is chronic edema usually accompanied by a history of pelvic surgery, malignancy or radiation therapy, none of which she has. Her symptoms began in the leg that had a deep vein thrombosis 11 months ago, within the 6 to 24 month window of post-thrombotic syndrome.
Drug-induced edema

Drug-induced edema, a common adverse effect of drugs such as amlodipine, is often bilateral and usually lacks signs of inflammation. Her swelling is one-sided, in the leg that had a clot 11 months ago, with brownish skin change, which points to post-thrombotic syndrome.
Post-thrombotic syndrome

Correct. Post-thrombotic (postphlebitic) syndrome is symptomatic chronic venous insufficiency that follows a deep vein thrombosis (DVT), from 6 to 24 months after the clot. Her left leg clot 11 months ago, followed by heaviness, edema and brownish ankle skin in that same leg, fits the window and the pattern.

opts: Ankle-brachial index

The ankle-brachial index is not part of the Wells pathway for a swollen leg. Her score of 3 (active cancer, entire leg swelling, calf swelling over 3 cm) is high, which leads to venous duplex ultrasound.
Venous duplex ultrasound

Correct. Active cancer on treatment 1 + entire leg swollen 1 + calf swelling over 3 cm 1 = 3, a high likelihood of deep vein thrombosis (DVT). A high-likelihood patient goes to ultrasound whatever a D-dimer shows, and duplex ultrasound has replaced venography.
D-dimer assay first
A D-dimer is the first test in the low-likelihood pathway, where a negative result ends the work-up. At a score of 3 her likelihood is high, so ultrasound is done whatever a D-dimer would show.
Contrast ascending venography
Contrast ascending venography is the definitive gold standard but has been replaced by venous duplex ultrasound. For a high Wells score, the next test is ultrasound, not venography.

opts: Ordering a venous duplex ultrasound

Ordering venous duplex ultrasound is exactly right: a high Wells score sends her to ultrasound whatever the D-dimer shows. Her negative result does not change that, so imaging is the step to take, not the one to avoid.
Asking about shortness of breath

Asking about shortness of breath is not a misstep in evaluating a suspected clot; it costs nothing and does not alter the Wells pathway. The action to avoid is ending the work-up at a negative D-dimer, since a high score goes on to ultrasound regardless.
Measuring both calf circumferences

Measuring both calves is how the Wells item for calf swelling is scored: more than 3 cm larger than the other leg, measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity. It is part of a correct evaluation, not an error.
Ending the work-up at the D-dimer

set1.q: A 66-year-old woman has a large arteriovenous fistula of the thigh and a positive Nicoladoni-Branham sign (slowing of the heart rate when the fistula is compressed). Her resting pulse is 88 beats per minute. Which action should the examiner avoid?
opts: Feeling for a thrill over it

Feeling for a thrill does not hold the fistula closed, so it does not provoke the reflex drop in heart rate. Physical examination is how an arteriovenous fistula is diagnosed; the maneuver to avoid is sustained compression of a large fistula.
Checking pulses below it

Checking the pulses below the fistula is part of a complete vascular examination and helps detect ischemia, one of the complications to watch for. It does not compress the fistula, so it carries no risk of the reflex slowing that compression causes.
Holding the fistula compressed

Correct. Her positive Nicoladoni-Branham sign means that compressing this large arteriovenous (AV) fistula reflexly slows her heart rate. Holding it compressed is the one action here that provokes that reflex, so sustained compression is what the examiner should avoid.
Listening over it for a bruit

Listening over the fistula does not compress it, so it cannot set off the reflex slowing of the heart. The diagnosis of an arteriovenous fistula is made by physical examination, and only compression of a large fistula triggers the Nicoladoni-Branham response.

Most accurate in hospitalized patients

This reverses the truth: the Wells score is less useful in hospitalized patients and is used only in the outpatient and emergency department settings. Six days in hospital places him in exactly the group it was not designed for.
Designed for upper-extremity clots

set1.q: A 71-year-old man has been on strict bed rest for six days during an admission for pneumonia and now has swelling and aching of the entire left leg. Which component of the Virchow triad does his prolonged bed rest represent?
opts: Endothelial trauma

Endothelial injury comes from trauma, surgery such as knee or hip replacement, intravenous drug use or burns. Bed rest during pneumonia does not injure the vein wall; it alters blood flow, which places it under venous stasis.
Arterial vasospasm

Arterial vasospasm is not one of the three Virchow components, which are venous stasis, a hypercoagulable state and vascular endothelial injury. His risk comes from immobilization, which the triad lists under venous stasis along with long flights and postoperative inactivity.
Venous stasis

Correct. Six days of strict bed rest is immobilization, which alters blood flow: the venous stasis arm of the Virchow triad. Immobilization carries about a 20-fold increased risk for deep vein thrombosis (DVT), which fits his new swelling and aching of the entire leg.
Hypercoagulable state

A hypercoagulable state is a clotting tendency, inherited (factor V Leiden, protein C or S deficiency) or acquired (cancer, estrogen, pregnancy). Lying still changes blood flow rather than the blood's clotting tendency, so his bed rest belongs to venous stasis.

set1.q: A 55-year-old man has a positive D-dimer during evaluation of calf pain two weeks after a bicycle crash with extensive bruising. He asks why his clinician says the result cannot confirm a clot. Which explanation is accurate?
opts: It rises only with pulmonary embolism

D-dimer is used as a rule-out test for both deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, so it is not tied to one disease. It reflects fibrinolysis, which is why a positive result in a man with recent extensive bruising cannot confirm a clot of any kind.
It rises only with thigh clots

D-dimer is a blood test that reflects fibrinolysis; it gives no location for a clot, in the thigh or anywhere else. Locating a thrombus takes imaging, which is why venous duplex ultrasound, which has replaced venography, follows a positive result.
It reflects fibrinolysis from many causes

Correct. An elevated D-dimer implies increased fibrinolysis, and the test is sensitive but not specific, so a positive result does not prove a deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Poor specificity means causes other than a clot, such as his recent crash with extensive bruising, can raise it; imaging is needed to confirm or exclude a clot.
It is specific but not sensitive

This reverses the test's profile: D-dimer is sensitive but not specific. Sensitivity is what lets a negative result help rule out a clot, and poor specificity is why his positive result needs venous duplex ultrasound before anyone calls it a deep vein thrombosis.

set1.q: A 63-year-old man with a peripherally inserted central catheter for chemotherapy develops a tender cord in the upper arm. Venous duplex ultrasound shows extensive clot burden in a superficial vein. He has active cancer and a prior deep vein thrombosis. Which therapy should be added to compresses and an anti-inflammatory drug?
opts: Aspirin alone

Aspirin alone is not among the agents used for this problem. With extensive clot burden or intermediate or higher thrombotic risk, as with his active cancer and prior clot, the added therapy is unfractionated heparin, enoxaparin or fondaparinux.
Anticoagulation

Correct. His duplex ultrasound shows extensive clot burden, and active cancer with a prior deep vein thrombosis puts him at higher risk of thrombosis. In that setting anticoagulation may be added to warm compresses and an anti-inflammatory drug, using unfractionated heparin, enoxaparin (a low molecular weight heparin) or fondaparinux.
Systemic corticosteroids

Systemic corticosteroids are not part of the treatment of superficial thrombophlebitis, which uses warm compresses, compression, elevation and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen. His extensive clot and high thrombotic risk call for anticoagulation instead.
Broad-spectrum antibiotics

Antibiotics are not part of the plan, since nothing in the stem describes infection within the vein. His ultrasound shows extensive clot, and with active cancer and a prior deep vein thrombosis the added treatment is anticoagulation with a heparin or fondaparinux.

set1.q: A 66-year-old woman has a painful ulcer above the medial malleolus with a clean base, fibrinous exudate and serous drainage, surrounded by brown pigmentation and pitting edema. Her pedal pulses are strong and her ankle-brachial index is 1.10. Which measure is essential for the ulcer to heal?
opts: Topical antibiotic dressings alone

Her ulcer has a clean base with fibrinous exudate, and a dressing alone does not address the cause. Venous ulcers will not heal unless edema is controlled and compression is applied; antibiotics are for cellulitis, given orally as cephalexin or clindamycin.
Oral flavonoid therapy alone

Flavonoids are used to increase venous tone, but no oral medication has yet been proven useful for venous disease. On its own a flavonoid will not heal the ulcer; edema control and compression are required.
Early surgical valvuloplasty

Valvuloplasty is only occasionally successful and carries a high incidence of postoperative deep vein thrombosis, so it is not the step that makes an ulcer heal. Healing requires edema control and compression, with wound care referral.
Compression with edema control

Correct. A painful ulcer above the medial malleolus with brown pigmentation and pitting edema is a venous ulcer, and venous ulcers will not heal unless edema is controlled and compression is applied. Wound care referral supports healing, which can take 4 to 6 months.

opts: Ligation of every communication

Ligating every communication is impractical because congenital fistulas can have numerous connections, which is exactly why they are difficult to treat. The initial approach is conservative, with elastic support hose, and embolization is sometimes used to remove the fistula.
Elastic support hose

Correct. A congenital arteriovenous (AV) fistula with numerous small communications is difficult to treat, so it is managed conservatively with elastic support hose. She has none of the complications to watch for, such as ischemia or heart failure, and embolization can sometimes remove a congenital fistula later.
Surgical excision of the fistula

Surgical removal or size reduction is the management for an acquired fistula, such as one from trauma or a procedure. Hers is congenital with numerous communications, which makes it difficult to treat, so elastic support hose comes first.
Lifelong anticoagulation

Anticoagulation does not treat an abnormal artery-to-vein connection, and her problem is not a clot. Congenital fistulas with numerous communications are treated conservatively with elastic support hose, with embolization as an occasional option.

opts: Acute myocardial infarction

Nothing in her story suggests a heart attack; the decisive clue is an untreated leg clot followed by sudden breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain. That sequence fits a fragment of thrombus breaking off and lodging in the lungs, a pulmonary embolism.
Pulmonary embolism

Correct. Part of a deep vein thrombus can break off and travel to the lungs, causing a pulmonary embolism. Her untreated leg clot followed by sudden shortness of breath and pleuritic chest pain fits that complication.
Post-thrombotic syndrome

Post-thrombotic syndrome is not a sudden chest event; it develops in the leg over time after a clot. Sudden shortness of breath and pleuritic chest pain in someone with an untreated leg clot point to a piece of thrombus traveling to the lungs.
Septic thrombophlebitis

Septic thrombophlebitis is an infection within a superficial vein and would not explain sudden breathlessness and pleuritic pain. Her known, untreated deep vein thrombosis is the source, with part of the clot traveling to the lungs as a pulmonary embolism.

opts: Reexamination in 24 to 48 hours

A recheck at 24 to 48 hours is too early to tell whether an uncomplicated superficial clot is resolving or progressing, and nothing in his course calls for urgent review. The scheduled repeat examination falls within 7 to 10 days, and only persistent or worsening signs at that visit lead to a repeat duplex ultrasound.
Reexamination in 7 to 10 days

Correct. His superficial thrombophlebitis is uncomplicated and already on the standard regimen of warm compresses, elevation and a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID). The next step is a repeat physical examination within 7 to 10 days to judge resolution versus progression; persistent or worsening signs then prompt a repeat duplex ultrasound.
Reexamination in 6 to 8 weeks

Six to 8 weeks leaves a possibly progressing clot unchecked far too long for a man just started on compresses, elevation and an anti-inflammatory drug. The repeat examination belongs within 7 to 10 days, when resolution versus progression can be judged and a repeat duplex ultrasound ordered if signs persist or worsen.
Return only if fever develops

Waiting for fever would miss a clot that persists or extends without infection, because progression is judged by examination, not by temperature. Management schedules a repeat examination within 7 to 10 days for everyone, with a repeat duplex ultrasound if the signs persist or worsen.

opts: Catheter-based venography

Correct. He is about to have an invasive venous procedure, and catheter-based (invasive) venography is the gold standard test, done before an invasive intervention. It is rarely needed to make the diagnosis of chronic venous insufficiency, which duplex ultrasound handles first.
Venous duplex ultrasound

Venous duplex ultrasound is the first test: it confirms the diagnosis, rules out deep vein thrombosis, finds reflux and determines the level and anatomy of disease. It is not the gold standard; catheter-based venography holds that role and is the test done before an invasive procedure.
Cross-sectional venography

Cross-sectional venography with computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging helps evaluate deep veins that ultrasound cannot properly detect. It is a supplementary study, not the gold standard, which is catheter-based venography performed before invasive intervention.
Ankle-brachial index

The ankle-brachial index (ABI) is paired with an arterial pulse examination for any patient with a lower extremity wound, especially older patients, to assess the arteries. It does not map venous anatomy, which catheter-based venography defines before an intervention.

Vein sclerotherapy

set1.q: A 64-year-old woman must stay in bed for several days after major abdominal surgery. Her team wants a preventive measure aimed at the venous stasis component of the Virchow triad. Which measure is most appropriate?
opts: Intermittent pneumatic compression

Correct. She will be immobilized in bed after major surgery, which is exactly when intermittent pneumatic compression is used to prevent deep vein thrombosis (DVT). The cuffs inflate in sequence from the lower leg upward, moving blood out of the leg and countering venous stasis.
Inferior vena cava filter

An inferior vena cava filter does not keep blood moving in the legs, so it does not address venous stasis. Prevention aimed at stasis in a bedbound postoperative patient is intermittent pneumatic compression.
Thrombolytic infusion

Thrombolysis with tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) treats an existing clot and is helpful for a large proximal deep vein thrombosis or a pulmonary embolism in a hemodynamically stable patient. She has no clot yet; preventing stasis after surgery calls for intermittent pneumatic compression.
Warm compresses to the calves

Warm compresses act on the skin and do nothing to keep blood moving in the deep veins of an immobilized leg. For a patient confined to bed after surgery, the preventive device is intermittent pneumatic compression, whose cuffs squeeze the leg in sequence.

opts: Confirm the skin over it is cool

A healthy fistula is expected to make a sound: a soft bruit with systolic and diastolic components, heard along with a diffuse thrill. Silence over the access is the opposite of the normal finding.
Feel for a vibrating thrill

Correct. A healthy arteriovenous (AV) fistula has a diffuse thrill and a soft bruit, both with systolic and diastolic components, so feeling the vibrating thrill over his forearm access is a simple check that it is working. Upper-extremity fistulas like his are created for long-term hemodialysis access.
Confirm it stays full when raised

A healthy fistula collapses completely when the arm is elevated, so an access that stays full when raised is not behaving normally. Collapse on elevation and a diffuse thrill with a soft bruit are the signs of a working fistula.

opts: Lymphedema of the arm

Heart failure

opts: Lymphedema

Correct. Bilateral, symmetric swelling just above the ankles in a woman is how lipedema is described. Her normal cardiac, kidney and liver evaluations exclude the systemic causes of bilateral edema, and the absence of varicose veins, ulcers or skin color change argues against venous disease.

set2.q: A 33-year-old woman eight weeks postpartum has mild calf aching and a low pretest probability of deep vein thrombosis. Her clinician orders a D-dimer. Which characteristic makes a negative result useful for excluding a clot?
opts: High specificity

D-dimer is sensitive but not specific, so a positive result cannot confirm a clot. Its value for excluding a clot in a low-probability patient like her comes from high sensitivity, which makes a negative result reliable.
Direct visualization of clot

D-dimer is a blood test whose elevation implies increased fibrinolysis; it does not visualize a clot. Seeing the thrombus is the job of venous duplex ultrasound, which has replaced contrast venography, while the D-dimer's value lies in its sensitivity.
Measurement of vein compressibility

A blood test cannot measure how a vein compresses; that would take imaging such as venous duplex ultrasound. D-dimer reflects fibrinolysis, and it excludes a clot in low-probability patients through its sensitivity.
High sensitivity

Correct. With a low pretest probability she starts with a D-dimer, and a negative result lets the clinician stop because the test is sensitive. Sensitivity is what makes it a rule-out test for deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism; it is not specific, so a positive result would still need ultrasound.

opts: Recurrence is rare after treatment

Only appearance improves, not symptoms

opts: Continue the same treatment

Continuing unchanged ignores the finding that matters: his cord has lengthened and the redness has spread at the 9-day recheck. Worsening signs at that visit call for a repeat duplex ultrasound, and an extensive clot would then justify anticoagulation.
Place an inferior vena cava filter

An inferior vena cava filter is not part of the management of superficial thrombophlebitis, which uses compresses, compression, elevation and anti-inflammatory drugs, with anticoagulation for extensive clot. His worsening signs call for a repeat duplex ultrasound first.
Reexamine again in four weeks

Another four-week wait would leave a worsening clot unassessed. The recheck at 7 to 10 days has already shown progression, and persistence or worsening at that point triggers a repeat duplex ultrasound, not a further delay.
Repeat duplex ultrasound

Correct. He had the standard recheck within 7 to 10 days, and the cord has lengthened and the redness spread, so his signs are worsening. Persistence or worsening at that recheck calls for a repeat duplex ultrasound; if it shows extensive clot burden, anticoagulation may be started.

opts: Superficial vein ablation

Ablation is a treatment for a known venous problem, and duplex ultrasound has not shown one here. With an ulcer whose cause remains unclear, the step is to establish the cause, which a punch biopsy can help do.
Catheter-based venography

Catheter-based venography is an invasive study of the veins and would not identify the nonvenous causes on the differential, such as autoimmune disease or erythema induratum. A punch biopsy is the tool for an ulcer of uncertain cause.
Punch biopsy

Correct. When the cause of a leg ulcer is uncertain, a punch biopsy can help rule out other causes. History and examination cannot reliably exclude other causes of a leg ulcer, and the differential includes autoimmune disease, sickle cell anemia and erythema induratum.

set2.q: A 63-year-old man with chronic venous insufficiency has two days of warmth, tenderness and spreading blanching redness of the lower leg, with a low-grade fever. Which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Oral flavonoid therapy

Flavonoids are used to increase venous tone, and no oral medication has yet been proven useful for venous disease itself. They do nothing for infection: his fever with spreading warm, tender redness is cellulitis, which is treated with oral cephalexin or clindamycin.
Oral cephalexin

Correct. Two days of warmth, tenderness and spreading blanching redness with a low-grade fever in a leg with chronic venous insufficiency describe cellulitis. Oral antibiotics are recommended for this cellulitis, and cephalexin or clindamycin are the named choices.
Topical antibiotic ointment

Cellulitis complicating chronic venous insufficiency calls for oral antibiotics, cephalexin or clindamycin, not a topical product. Topical care in this setting means cleansers, emollients and barrier creams for stasis dermatitis; his fever and spreading warmth mark an infection that needs an oral drug.

Mid-potency topical corticosteroids such as triamcinolone treat the erythema, inflammation, itching and vesicles of stasis dermatitis. set2.q: A 49-year-old man has a first proximal deep vein thrombosis with no surgery, trauma, hormone use, travel, cancer or other identifiable trigger, and no inherited disorder has been found. How long should anticoagulation continue?
opts: Three to six months

Three to six months is for a clot provoked by a minor transient factor such as estrogen therapy, pregnancy, minor surgery, prolonged travel or minor leg injury. He has none of these; with no identifiable trigger, treatment is indefinite.
Six weeks
Six weeks is shorter than the minimum, since every acute first venous thromboembolism is treated for at least 3 months. An unprovoked first clot like his goes further still, to indefinite treatment.
Indefinitely

Correct. His first proximal deep vein thrombosis had no surgery, trauma, hormones, travel, cancer or other trigger, which makes it an unprovoked first venous thromboembolism (VTE). An unprovoked first VTE is treated for an indefinite length of time, beyond the 3-month minimum that applies to every first episode.

Three months is the course for a clot provoked by a major transient factor, such as surgery under general anesthesia over 30 minutes, 3 or more days of bed rest, or major trauma or fracture. He had no trigger, so his unprovoked clot is treated indefinitely.

opts: Skin emollients

Emollients such as Vaseline or Lubriderm maintain the skin barrier, preventing dryness and fissuring and decreasing scratching. They put no pressure on the leg, so arterial disease is no reason to hold them; compression is the treatment that waits.
Graduated compression

Correct. Compression therapy is the standard treatment for venous insufficiency, but peripheral artery disease must be ruled out before it is initiated. Her weak pedal pulses and ankle-brachial index of 0.6 point to arterial disease, so graduated compression waits until that is addressed.
Gentle skin cleansing

opts: Its bruit turns systolic only
A healthy fistula's bruit has both systolic and diastolic components, so a systolic-only bruit is not the healthy pattern. The expected response to elevation is complete collapse of the fistula.
It collapses completely

Correct. A healthy arteriovenous (AV) fistula collapses completely when the arm is elevated. It is also generally characterized by a diffuse thrill and a soft bruit, both with systolic and diastolic components.
It stays distended and tense
Staying distended and tense when the arm is raised is not the healthy response. A healthy fistula collapses completely with arm elevation, alongside a diffuse thrill and a soft bruit.
Her heart rate slows
Slowing of the heart rate is the Nicoladoni-Branham sign, a reflex to compression of a large fistula, not a response to raising the arm. A healthy fistula collapses completely with elevation.

Observation without treatment

opts: Clot within the vein lumen

Correct. The ultrasound already shows wall thickening, which by itself means phlebitis, inflammation of the vein wall without thrombus. Clot within the vein together with that thickening establishes thrombophlebitis; duplex ultrasound, the gold standard, shows it as a noncompressible superficial vein with clot.
Thickening of the vein wall

opts: Elevated platelet count

An elevated platelet count is not one of the three Virchow components, which are venous stasis, a hypercoagulable state and endothelial injury. Heart failure is placed under venous stasis, the component of altered blood flow.
Venous stasis

Correct. Heart failure is listed under venous stasis, the Virchow triad component of altered blood flow, alongside immobilization and venous insufficiency. Her heart failure raises clot risk through stasis; it is neither an injury to the vein wall nor an inherited or acquired clotting tendency.
Hypercoagulable state

A hypercoagulable state is a clotting tendency, inherited (factor V Leiden, protein C or S deficiency) or acquired (cancer, estrogen, pregnancy). Heart failure is grouped instead with immobilization and venous insufficiency under venous stasis, the altered blood flow component.

Endothelial injury comes from trauma, surgery, intravenous drug use or burns. Heart failure does not damage the vessel lining; it is listed under venous stasis, the component of altered blood flow.

opts: Overlapping heparin with warfarin

Overlapping heparin with warfarin is the standard plan: unfractionated heparin continues alongside warfarin for at least 5 days and until the international normalized ratio is above 2 for at least 24 hours. It is part of her inpatient treatment, not an error.
Beginning therapy as an outpatient

Correct. With a creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min, she needs to be hospitalized to start treatment, so beginning therapy at home is the approach to avoid. In hospital she receives unfractionated heparin (UFH) as an intravenous bolus followed by a continuous infusion, adjusted by laboratory results and overlapped with warfarin.
Admission for intravenous heparin

Admission is exactly what a creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min requires: she is hospitalized and given unfractionated heparin as an intravenous loading bolus followed by a continuous infusion. This is the recommended plan, not one to avoid.
Adjusting heparin by lab results

Adjusting the dose by laboratory results is standard for unfractionated heparin, which is titrated to the activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT). That monitoring is part of the inpatient plan her kidney function requires, so it is not the approach to avoid.

set2.q: A 45-year-old man with a first deep vein thrombosis is otherwise healthy and hemodynamically stable. The plan is oral anticoagulation monotherapy with a loading phase followed by maintenance, without any injection lead-in. Which drug fits this strategy?
opts: Dabigatran

Dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor, is started after 5 days of parenteral therapy, so it requires the injection lead-in this plan avoids. Oral monotherapy with a loading dose then maintenance uses rivaroxaban or apixaban.
Edoxaban

Edoxaban is an anti-Xa agent, but it belongs to the strategy in which parenteral therapy is switched after 5 days to a novel anticoagulant. The plan here has no injection lead-in, which means rivaroxaban or apixaban.
Fondaparinux

Fondaparinux is an indirect factor Xa inhibitor, not one of the two oral agents used for monotherapy. The oral strategy with a loading dose followed by maintenance, with no injection lead-in, uses rivaroxaban or apixaban.
Apixaban

Correct. Oral monotherapy with a loading dose followed by a maintenance dose, with no injection lead-in, is the strategy that uses rivaroxaban or apixaban, both anti-Xa agents. Apixaban (Eliquis) is a direct factor Xa inhibitor, and he is stable and otherwise healthy, so the oral-only plan fits.

set2.q: A 55-year-old woman had femoral vessel puncture for an endovascular procedure two days ago. Examination of the groin shows a new bruit over the puncture site, and the surgeon suspects an iatrogenic arteriovenous fistula. Which study is used to confirm the diagnosis?
opts: D-dimer assay

A D-dimer is a blood test and gives no picture of the vessels at the puncture site, so it cannot show an abnormal artery-to-vein connection. Confirming a suspected iatrogenic fistula after femoral access takes duplex ultrasound.
Ankle-brachial index

The ankle-brachial index is not used to confirm an arteriovenous fistula. After groin access, the puncture site is checked with a complete lower extremity vascular examination comparing pulses with pre-procedure findings, and a suspected fistula is confirmed by duplex ultrasound.
Plain radiograph of the groin

A plain radiograph is not among the tests used to confirm an arteriovenous fistula. After femoral access, a suspected iatrogenic fistula is confirmed with duplex ultrasound, and computed tomography angiography or angiography can add its location and size.
Duplex ultrasound

Correct. Puncture of the femoral vessels for an endovascular procedure is the classic setting for an iatrogenic arteriovenous (AV) fistula, and duplex ultrasound confirms the diagnosis in suspected cases. Computed tomography angiography and angiography can also confirm a fistula and show its location and size.

set2.q: A 62-year-old woman receiving chemotherapy through a central venous catheter has two days of right arm swelling and aching. The catheter injuring the vein wall is the endothelial trauma component of the Virchow triad. Which is the best diagnostic test?
opts: Venous duplex ultrasound

Correct. Two days of arm swelling and aching with a central venous catheter call for imaging of that limb, and venous duplex ultrasound of the involved extremity is the test that has replaced contrast venography for deep vein thrombosis (DVT). A D-dimer could not confirm the clot, because it is sensitive but not specific.
Contrast ascending venography

Contrast ascending venography is the definitive gold standard for deep vein thrombosis, but it has been replaced by venous duplex ultrasound of the involved extremity. It is not where her work-up starts; the noninvasive ultrasound is.
Ankle-brachial index

The ankle-brachial index is not a venous imaging test and plays no part in diagnosing deep vein thrombosis, which rests on venous duplex ultrasound of the involved extremity. Her swollen arm with an indwelling catheter needs that ultrasound to show the clot.
D-dimer alone

D-dimer is sensitive but not specific: elevation implies fibrinolysis, so a positive result cannot confirm a clot, and the test is used to rule out rather than diagnose. With arm swelling around a catheter she needs venous duplex ultrasound of the arm to show the thrombus.

set2.q: A 60-year-old man has had untreated varicose veins for many years. He now has persistent lower leg swelling, brown skin discoloration and a shallow ulcer above the medial ankle. Untreated long-standing varicose veins can progress to which condition?
opts: Lymphedema

Lymphedema is not described as a progression of varicose veins. The condition long-standing varicose veins can progress to is chronic venous insufficiency, which fits his swelling, brown discoloration and medial ankle ulcer.
Arteriovenous fistula

An arteriovenous fistula is not a progression of varicose veins. Long-standing varicose veins can progress to chronic venous insufficiency, which explains persistent swelling, brown discoloration and an ulcer above the medial ankle.
Chronic venous insufficiency

Correct. Long-standing varicose veins can progress to chronic venous insufficiency. His persistent swelling, brown skin discoloration and shallow ulcer above the medial ankle after years of untreated varicose veins fit that progression.
Peripheral artery disease

Peripheral artery disease is not a progression of venous disease. Long-standing varicose veins can progress to chronic venous insufficiency, the explanation for his persistent swelling, brown discoloration and medial ankle ulcer.

set2.q: A 32-year-old woman who is 34 weeks pregnant sits in a car for nine hours and develops left calf swelling and pain. Her pregnancy supplies a hypercoagulable state and the long ride supplies venous stasis. Which additional component would complete the Virchow triad?
opts: Endothelial trauma

Correct. The Virchow triad is venous stasis, a hypercoagulable state and vascular endothelial injury. Her pregnancy supplies the hypercoagulable state and nine hours in a car supply stasis, so the missing third is endothelial trauma, as from trauma, surgery, intravenous drug use or burns.
Venous stasis

Venous stasis is already present: nine hours of sitting in a car is immobilization, like a long flight. The question asks for the component not yet supplied, which is endothelial trauma, injury to the vessel lining.
Hypercoagulable state

Pregnancy is already listed as a hypercoagulable state, so that component is present, not missing. With stasis from the car ride also present, the third component still needed is endothelial trauma, injury to the vessel wall.
Arterial thrombosis

Arterial thrombosis is not a component of the Virchow triad, whose three elements are venous stasis, a hypercoagulable state and vascular endothelial injury. With stasis and hypercoagulability already present, the missing element is endothelial trauma.

set2.q: A 61-year-old man receiving chemotherapy for lung cancer has had swelling of his whole left leg for four days, with pitting edema in that leg and a calf 4 cm larger than the right. An ultrasound of the thigh veins shows no clot. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Repeat the thigh scan in a week

Correct. Active cancer 1 + entire leg swollen 1 + calf swelling over 3 cm 1 + pitting edema in the symptomatic leg 1 = 4, a high likelihood. In the high-likelihood pathway a negative thigh ultrasound is followed by a lower leg ultrasound, phlebography or a repeat thigh ultrasound in 1 week.
Stop the work-up; clot excluded

Stopping after a negative thigh ultrasound belongs to the low-likelihood pathway. His score of 4 (active cancer, entire leg swelling, calf swelling over 3 cm, pitting edema) is high, so a negative thigh study needs follow-up imaging.
Start anticoagulation for life
Anticoagulation is the mainstay of treatment once a deep vein thrombosis is found, but none has been shown yet. A high-likelihood patient with a negative thigh ultrasound needs further imaging first.
Ankle-brachial index

The ankle-brachial index is not part of the deep vein thrombosis pathway. After a negative thigh ultrasound in a high-likelihood patient, imaging continues with a lower leg ultrasound, phlebography or a repeat thigh scan in 1 week.

set2.q: A 36-year-old woman who smokes and takes an oral contraceptive has mild calf aching. Her Wells score is low, and her D-dimer returns positive. What is the next step?
opts: Venous duplex ultrasound

Correct. Her Wells score is low, so she started with a D-dimer, and a positive result leads on to ultrasound. D-dimer is sensitive but not specific, so it cannot confirm a clot, and venous duplex ultrasound has replaced contrast venography for diagnosis.
Empiric anticoagulation alone

Empiric anticoagulation would treat a clot that has not been shown; a positive D-dimer implies fibrinolysis but is not specific for deep vein thrombosis. In the low-likelihood pathway a positive result leads to ultrasound, which decides whether treatment is needed.
Reassurance and discharge

Reassurance and discharge are for a negative D-dimer in a low-likelihood patient. Her result is positive, and because the test is not specific, ultrasound is needed to find out whether a clot is present.
Repeat D-dimer tomorrow

Repeating a test that is sensitive but not specific cannot settle whether a clot is present. In the low-likelihood pathway a positive D-dimer moves straight to ultrasound, which has replaced venography for diagnosis.

set2.q: A 76-year-old man has had symmetric pitting swelling of both ankles for three weeks. He started amlodipine for hypertension one month ago. There is no warmth, redness, tenderness or skin discoloration, and he has no history of heart, kidney or liver disease. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Chronic venous insufficiency

Chronic venous insufficiency in its post-thrombotic form follows a deep vein thrombosis by 6 to 24 months, and he has no history of a clot. His swelling is only three weeks old, bilateral, without skin discoloration, and began after amlodipine, which fits drug-induced edema.
Lymphedema

Lymphedema is chronic edema of the extremities, usually with a history of pelvic surgery, malignancy or radiation therapy, none of which he has. The timing is the tell: his swelling started weeks after amlodipine was begun and is bilateral without inflammation, the pattern of drug-induced edema.
Drug-induced edema

Correct. Symmetric pitting swelling of both ankles that began after starting amlodipine, with no warmth, redness or tenderness, fits drug-induced edema. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine commonly cause it; the swelling is often bilateral and usually shows no signs of inflammation.
Bilateral deep vein thrombosis

Drug-induced edema sits on the differential of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) because it swells the legs, but it is often bilateral and usually lacks signs of inflammation. His symmetric swelling without warmth, redness or tenderness began a month after amlodipine, which points to the drug rather than clots in both legs.

set2.q: A 57-year-old man with knee osteoarthritis felt a sudden sharp pain behind the right knee while climbing stairs, followed by severe calf discomfort and swelling. Venous duplex ultrasound shows no thrombus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Superficial thrombophlebitis

Superficial thrombophlebitis is a clot in a superficial vein, not a sudden event that starts behind the knee during exertion. The tell is the abrupt pain behind the knee followed by severe calf discomfort with a clot-free ultrasound, which on the differential of deep vein thrombosis belongs to a ruptured popliteal (Baker) cyst.
Ruptured popliteal (Baker) cyst

Correct. Sudden pain behind the knee followed by severe, sudden calf discomfort and swelling, with a duplex ultrasound that shows no thrombus, fits a ruptured popliteal (Baker) cyst. It sits on the differential of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) because it mimics the swollen, painful calf of a clot.
Calf muscle tear

A calf muscle pull or tear usually has an inciting injury in the history and may leave bruising at the ankle. Climbing stairs is ordinary activity and he has no bruising; pain that began behind the knee and then became severe calf discomfort favors a ruptured popliteal (Baker) cyst.
Post-thrombotic syndrome

Post-thrombotic (postphlebitic) syndrome is symptomatic chronic venous insufficiency that follows a deep vein thrombosis by 6 to 24 months. He has no prior clot and his symptoms began suddenly, so a chronic after-clot process does not fit; abrupt onset behind the knee is the tell for a ruptured cyst.

set2.q: A 66-year-old man taking apixaban for deep vein thrombosis develops an acute intracranial hemorrhage. Which agent reverses the anticoagulant?
opts: Andexanet alfa

Correct. He is taking apixaban and has an acute intracranial hemorrhage, one of the situations that calls for reversal. Andexanet alfa (Andexxa) is the reversal agent for apixaban and rivaroxaban, and it is used off-label for edoxaban.
Protamine sulfate
Protamine sulfate reverses unfractionated heparin and low molecular weight heparin. He takes apixaban, so the reversal agent for his intracranial hemorrhage is andexanet alfa.
Idarucizumab
Idarucizumab is the reversal agent for dabigatran and does not act on apixaban. For his intracranial bleed on apixaban, the reversal agent is andexanet alfa, the same agent used for rivaroxaban.
Vitamin K by mouth

Oral vitamin K is one of the reversal options for warfarin, along with prothrombin complex concentrate, fresh frozen plasma and intravenous vitamin K. He takes apixaban, whose reversal agent is andexanet alfa.
